analysis.one_liner: Writes net neutrality into law, banning internet providers from blocking, slowing, or charging websites extra to reach users.
analysis.headline: The net neutrality bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Internet Freedom Preservation Act of 2009 would have made net neutrality a legal duty. Internet providers — mostly the local cable and telephone companies — could no longer block or slow down websites, charge online companies extra fees for faster delivery, force customers into bundles, or stop people from using the devices of their choice. The Federal Communications Commission would have had to write enforcement rules within months, including a fast complaint process for users. The bill was introduced by Rep. Edward Markey with 27 cosponsors, all Democrats, but was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittees and never received a vote in committee or on the House floor before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet at home or work. The bill guaranteed that the companies controlling residential broadband — mostly the local cable and telephone companies, which the bill notes face each other as the only two wireline choices for most households — could not block or slow lawful websites, charge websites and apps extra for faster delivery, or force customers into bundles. Small online businesses, startups, video streaming services, and independent creators would benefit most directly, since they could reach users without paying the broadband provider a toll. Consumers also would have gained a right to attach any lawful device and to clear disclosure of speeds and network practices, plus an FCC complaint process.

how_it_helps.text: It made it the legal duty of every internet provider not to block, interfere with, discriminate against, impair, or degrade anyone's ability to use the internet to reach lawful content, applications, or services.

It banned providers from charging websites and online services extra fees for faster or guaranteed delivery, which would have prevented a two-tiered internet where deep-pocketed companies buy priority and everyone else is left behind.
It protected customers' right to hook up any lawful device — a router, a home network, their choice of equipment — as long as it did not harm the provider's network.

It barred providers from forcing customers to buy bundled packages, requiring the FCC to write rules within 180 days so no one could be made to purchase other services as a condition of getting internet access.

It required providers to disclose their speed, network management practices, and service limitations clearly to consumers, and set up an FCC complaint process with 90-day resolution so users could challenge violations.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers — the cable and telephone companies — would bear the cost: they could no longer sell paid fast lanes to content companies, could not favor their own video and voice services over rivals, and would face FCC enforcement, damages orders to complaining parties, and disclosure requirements. Some of that lost gatekeeping revenue had been flowing from websites and app companies, and could otherwise have been passed on to consumers or to online services' customers.

drawbacks.text: The bill let internet providers engage in 'reasonable network management' — practices that serve a critically important interest, are narrowly tailored, and are the least restrictive option — but deciding which practices qualify would fall to FCC regulators, creating uncertainty for providers and possible delays in legitimate traffic management.

Broadband providers argued that bright-line bans on charging content companies for faster delivery could discourage the multi-billion-dollar investments needed to expand and upgrade networks, a cost that could eventually reach consumers — the bill itself acknowledged the need to promote 'an ever-increasing level of Internet access service' and ample network capacity.
The bill required the FCC to write sweeping rules within 90 days of enactment and to resolve complaints within 90 days, an unusually tight timeline that could have produced rushed regulations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — keeping the internet open so that no company can slow a rival's video service or charge websites a toll to reach customers — is large and touches nearly everyone, since most households had only one cable and one phone company to choose from. The main cost falls on broadband providers, who argued that strict nondiscrimination rules could discourage investment in network upgrades and that legitimate traffic-management was needed; the bill tried to address that by allowing "reasonable network management" that is narrowly tailored and by requiring the FCC to consider each network's technical limits. A fair objection is that writing these rules into statute, with a 90-day rulemaking deadline, risked locking in rules that technology would quickly outgrow. On balance, the bill's benefits to consumers and small online businesses outweighed that risk, and the bill's death left the cable and telephone companies' gatekeeper position intact.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittees and never advanced to a markup or a floor vote, so it expired when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey, joined by Rep. Anna Eshoo, introduced the Internet Freedom Preservation Act of 2009 on July 31, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

On September 8, 2009, the bill was referred to two Energy and Commerce subcommittees — Communications, Technology, and the Internet, and Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection — and no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill attracted 27 cosponsors, all House Democrats, but never received a committee vote or a House floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers — the cable and telephone companies that control home internet access — came out ahead, keeping their ability to manage, prioritize, and charge for traffic without statutory limits. Everyday internet users gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its net neutrality duties for internet providers.

for.name: Rep. Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Joined Markey in introducing the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a markup; after subcommittee referral on September 8, 2009, no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Broadband and cable industry
against.what_they_did: Fiercely opposed net neutrality legislation and lobbied against FCC open-internet rules throughout this period, arguing regulation would discourage network investment.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were Democrats and the Democratic leadership controlled the House, but the bill stalled inside a Democratic-run committee without ever drawing a floor vote, so its death was a matter of inaction rather than a party-line roll call.

industries.industry: Broadband internet providers (cable and telephone companies)
industries.note: The bill's duties fell directly on the companies that control residential internet access, banning paid priority for content companies, blocking or degrading rival services, forced bundling, and device restrictions. With most consumers able to choose only between the local cable and telephone company [S3], these rules would have ended the industry's ability to act as a toll-taker on internet traffic.

industries.industry: Internet content, application, and service companies
industries.note: Everything from video streaming services to small startups would gain a legal guarantee that they can reach customers without paying the broadband provider for priority or being slowed in favor of the provider's own competing services. The bill's findings stress that these providers' ability to reach consumers depends on open networks.

Not an industry but the chief beneficiary: the bill guaranteed open access, honest disclosure of speeds and limits, the right to attach any lawful device, and no forced bundling. The costs of the bill's failure fall on the same group, since the cable-telephone duopoly kept its gatekeeping power.
